subtype: Signing a tiny pledge, then being asked for more [Receiver]
passage:
Monday: Ojas clicked "I pledge to reduce plastic" on a campaign page. Just a name and an email. It felt good.
Wednesday: An email arrived: "Thank you, Ojas! Pledge-takers like you share with five friends." He forwarded it to five people, including Trisha.
Saturday: Another email: "Committed members like you volunteer for our weekend drive, collecting donations door to door. Can we count on you?" Ojas's stomach tightened. He had exams next week. But he was a pledge-taker now, a "committed member." Saying no felt like being a fake. He typed "Yes" and hovered over send. Trisha, reading over his shoulder, said, "You clicked one box on Monday. Would you have said yes if this was the first thing they asked?" Ojas deleted the "Yes."

qa.q: What did Ojas click on Monday?
Why did saying no on Saturday feel like "being a fake" to Ojas?
qa.a: He felt guilty and trapped: the emails called him a "committed member", so refusing seemed inconsistent with who he had claimed to be, even with exams next week.

qa.q: What question turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Trisha asked whether he would have said yes if this had been the first request; it separated the big ask from the small box he clicked on Monday.

qa.q: How might Trisha see the campaign's emails?
qa.a: Trisha, who received the forward, seems to notice how each email builds on the last to make the next ask feel natural, and cares enough to point it out.

grounding: A teenager who agreed to a small online pledge finds the larger follow-up hard to refuse, because saying no feels inconsistent with his earlier yes.

subtype: Signing a tiny pledge, then being asked for more [Receiver]
passage: Kiran, before you sign up for more of those online challenges, hear your Baljeet Mama's story. At sixteen, I had just made my first email ID at the cyber café. A site asked me to sign an online pledge to "stand with farmers." One click. Easy. A week later they wrote, "As a pledger, will you donate fifty rupees?" Fifty rupees was my whole week's money, but how could a pledger say no? I paid. Then they asked me to get ten classmates to pay too, and to send my father's phone number for "updates." That's when my stomach turned. I told my father that same evening, and he asked, "Would you have given fifty rupees and my number to strangers on the first day?" No. Each yes had made the next one feel owed.

qa.q: How much did the site ask Baljeet to donate?
Why did young Baljeet feel he couldn't refuse the donation?
qa.a: Baljeet felt torn and pressured: fifty rupees was his whole week's money, but having signed the pledge, saying no felt wrong for a "pledger".

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did young Baljeet do right?
qa.a: When they asked for his father's phone number, he felt uneasy and told his father that evening, whose question showed he would never have agreed on the first day.

qa.q: How might Baljeet's father have felt hearing about the requests?
qa.a: He may have been concerned that strangers wanted his number and his son's classmates' money, but he helped calmly with a simple question.

grounding: An uncle recalls how, as a teenager, a one-click online pledge made a bigger follow-up request feel impossible to refuse.

subtype: Signing a tiny pledge, then being asked for more [Receiver]
passage: The wedding sangeet was deafening, Nilesh's phone was at six percent, and a notification said "Offer ends in 5 minutes." Last week he had tapped "I pledge: one screen-free hour a day" on a wellness page. Tiny, easy. Now they wrote: "Pledgers like you are serious about change. Get our 30-day Focus Journal, ₹499, only for committed members." Nilesh had exactly ₹600 of wedding gift money. Not buying felt like breaking his pledge. His thumb hovered. His cousin Tarun leaned over, shouting over the dhol, "What's that?" "I pledged. So I sort of have to." Tarun shouted back, "You pledged an hour off screens. Not ₹499!" The phone died in Nilesh's hand. He laughed, a bit relieved, and went to dance.

qa.q: How much was the Focus Journal?
Why did not buying the journal feel like breaking a pledge to Nilesh?
qa.a: The page called him a "committed member", so after the small pledge, refusing the bigger request felt inconsistent with who he had said he was.

qa.q: What point did Tarun make, and how could Nilesh use it next time?
qa.a: That the pledge was an hour off screens, not ₹499; next time Nilesh can ask whether he would agree to the new request if it were the first one.

qa.q: How might Tarun see the offer from outside?
qa.a: To Tarun, it is obvious the ₹499 journal has nothing to do with a screen-free hour; without the pledge feeling, the ask looks like plain selling.

grounding: A teenager who made a small online pledge feels bound to buy a pricier follow-up offer, because refusing seems inconsistent with his earlier yes.

subtype: Signing a tiny pledge, then being asked for more [Receiver]
passage: In her Bhopal flat, Indu, fifteen, clicked 'I pledge to protect our lakes' on a campaign page. Name, email, done. It felt nice. Two days later, an email: 'Thank you, lake protector! Share this on your story.' She did. After all, she was a lake protector now. A week later: 'Protectors like you are recruiting ten friends. And get our campaign T-shirt, ₹350.' Indu looked at her pocket money tin. She had ₹400, saved for a birthday gift for Payal. But how could a lake protector say no? She messaged Payal: 'Would it be weird if I don't buy it?' Payal replied, 'You signed a pledge, not a contract.' Indu read the email again. 'Protectors like you.' She felt a little cornered, as if saying no would make her a fake. She hovered over the pay button for a long time.

qa.q: How much did the campaign T-shirt cost?
Why did Indu feel cornered by the email?
qa.a: Having pledged and called herself a lake protector, she felt trapped and uneasy, as if saying no would prove she was fake, even though she wanted the money for Payal's gift.

qa.q: What could Indu ask herself before paying, and why would it help?
qa.a: She could ask whether she would buy the T-shirt if that had been the first request, which would separate the new ask from her earlier small yes.

qa.q: How does Payal see the pledge?
qa.a: Payal sees it as a pledge, not a contract, meaning Indu can care about lakes and still say no to the T-shirt.

grounding: A teenage girl who clicked a small online pledge finds it hard to refuse a bigger follow-up request, because saying no feels inconsistent with the label she accepted.

subtype: Signing a tiny pledge, then being asked for more [Receiver]
passage:
'Ira, I have to buy the reading app's yearly plan.'
'Have to?'
'I took the ten-minutes-a-day pledge last month. I have a badge. "Committed Reader."'
'So?'
'So now it says, "Committed readers unlock unlimited books. ₹999 for a year."'
'That's a lot of pocket money, Aadhya Didi.'
'But I'm a committed reader. It says so.'
'You read from the library.'
'That's different.'
'How?'
'If I don't buy it, then I wasn't really committed. Then the pledge was fake.'
'Would you have paid ₹999 if they'd asked you first?'
Aadhya was quiet. 'No. Obviously not.'
'So?'
'So it's different now. I said yes already.'
'To ten minutes. Not to ₹999.'
Aadhya looked at the badge on her screen. 'It still feels rude to say no.'
'To a phone?'
Aadhya laughed, but she didn't close the app.

qa.q: How much was the reading app's yearly plan?
Why did Aadhya feel she 'had to' buy the plan?
qa.a: She felt guilty about refusing, because after the pledge and the 'Committed Reader' badge, saying no seemed like admitting the pledge was fake.

qa.q: Which question from Ira was the turning point, and what could Aadhya do with it?
qa.a: Ira asked whether Aadhya would have paid ₹999 if asked first; Aadhya could use that answer, no, to decline the plan while keeping her reading habit.

qa.q: How does Ira see the app's request?
qa.a: Ira sees that the pledge was for ten minutes a day, not ₹999, and finds it odd that saying no to a phone could feel rude.

grounding: At home a teenage girl feels bound to buy a costly app plan after taking a tiny reading pledge, as refusing now feels inconsistent with being a committed reader.
